analysis.one_liner: Lets shooting victims sue gun makers and sellers, ending their federal lawsuit immunity.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor vote in the House and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2005 law, the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, blocks most lawsuits against gun and ammunition makers, sellers, and their trade association when someone misuses a firearm. This bill would repeal that shield, letting victims of gun violence sue the industry in state and federal court like victims of other products can. It would also make federal gun-trace data usable as evidence in those lawsuits. The bill was introduced in October 2017, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, referred to a subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of gun violence and their families, who would gain the right to sue manufacturers, dealers, and sellers in civil court for harms from criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm, and potentially win damages or force safer business practices through discovery of trace data. Cities and states pursuing gun-industry litigation would also regain a legal avenue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun violence victims and their families

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the core provisions of the 2005 Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act (sections 2 through 4), which currently bar most civil suits against firearm or ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and trade associations for criminal or unlawful misuse of a gun [S2] [S3].

Makes the ATF's Firearms Trace System database subject to subpoenas and admissible as evidence in civil and administrative proceedings, so plaintiffs could use government trace data to show how guns reached the black market [S2] [S3].

Would put gun industry defendants in roughly the same legal position as other product makers, whose customers can sue them when a product is misused, ending a carve-out unique to the firearm trade [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, importers, sellers, and their trade associations, which would face civil lawsuits, litigation costs, and potential damages for unlawful misuse of their products, and possibly higher prices or tighter sales practices passed on to buyers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun and ammunition makers and dealers

drawbacks.text: Opponents of repealing the 2005 law argue that sellers and manufacturers cannot control criminals who steal or illegally resell guns, and that exposing them to lawsuits for third-party crimes could impose crushing litigation costs on lawful businesses, including small gun shops, and push some out of the market [S3].

The legal exposure created by the bill would be broad: it restores suits not just for defective products but for lawful sales later misused, so the industry would face costs tied to conduct it did not itself engage in [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to victims is real but indirect: this is an access-to-courts bill, not a direct safety measure, and any deterrence depends on lawsuits actually succeeding after the fact. The cost falls heavily on the gun industry and could mean higher prices and litigation risk for small dealers. Whether that trade is worth it turns on whether one thinks a special federal immunity for one industry is justified; the bill's core case is that no other consumer product enjoys this shield.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its Constitution subcommittee for the rest of the two-year Congress and was never brought to a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Adam Schiff introduced the bill on October 5, 2017, joined by 45 Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S4].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on October 5, 2017, and to the Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice on October 16, 2017 [S5].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the action history before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and their trade association are better off, because the federal liability shield created by the 2005 Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act remains intact and they cannot be sued for criminal misuse of their products. Gun violence victims remain without the courtroom access the bill would have restored.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun manufacturers and dealers, who keep immunity

for.name: Rep. Adam Schiff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the gun industry's liability shield and open ATF trace data to civil discovery.

for.name: 45 of 194 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 45 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee that received the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill stayed at the subcommittee referral stage until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 46 supporters (the sponsor plus 45 cosponsors) were House Democrats, and the Republican-run committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would repeal the 2005 law that shields them from most civil suits arising from criminal misuse of firearms. Their interest in keeping the shield runs against victims' interest in suing, because the shield's whole effect is to close off those claims.

industries.industry: Gun dealers, sellers, importers, and trade associations
industries.note: They are covered by the same liability immunity, and the bill would expose them to lawsuits for unlawful sales and diversion. Industry groups have defended the shield as protection from being blamed for third-party crimes.
